title: Place n queens on an n×n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and return all distinct solutions (or the count).
shortTitle: N-Queens — place queens row by row, check conflicts

s1_definition.profdef: Backtrack one row at a time, trying each column in the current row and placing a queen only where no existing queen shares the column or either diagonal. Track occupied columns and both diagonal families (row−col and row+col) in sets for O(1) conflict checks. When all n rows are filled, record the board configuration.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine placing n non-conflicting audit checkpoints on an n-by-n schedule grid where no two checkpoints may share a column or a diagonal time-slot. You fill one row at a time, placing a checkpoint only in a safe column, and backtrack whenever a row has no safe spot.
s1_definition.oneliner: One queen per row; a column is safe if its column and both diagonals are free; backtrack when a row is stuck.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtrack one row at a time, trying each column in the current row and placing a queen only where no existing queen shares the column or either diagonal. Track occupied columns and both diagonal families (row−col and row+col) in sets for O(1) conflict checks. When all n rows are filled, record the board configuration.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine placing n non-conflicting audit checkpoints on an n-by-n schedule grid where no two checkpoints may share a column or a diagonal time-slot. You fill one row at a time, placing a checkpoint only in a safe column, and backtrack whenever a row has no safe spot.

**One line to remember:** One queen per row; a column is safe if its column and both diagonals are free; backtrack when a row is stuck.

sections.s2_technical:
Recurse by row. For each column in the row, check three sets: used columns, the "down-right" diagonal keyed by row−col, and the "down-left" diagonal keyed by row+col. If all are free, place the queen (add keys), recurse to the next row, then remove the keys. For example: `if (!cols.contains(c) && !diag1.contains(r-c) && !diag2.contains(r+c)) { place; backtrack(r+1); unplace; }`.

Using row−col and row+col as diagonal identifiers gives constant-time conflict checks, which is far faster than scanning the board each time. When the row index reaches n, a full valid placement exists and is recorded.

The time is bounded by the branching of columns per row with heavy pruning, far below n to the n in practice. A senior nuance is that the two diagonal invariants (difference constant and sum constant) are the key insight that makes the conflict test O(1).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, n audit checkpoints must be placed on an n-by-n scheduling grid so that no two conflict by column or diagonal time-slot, and compliance wants every valid arrangement. This is exactly how N-Queens works.

Problem 2 — Placement proceeds one row at a time and must backtrack when a row has no safe column. This is exactly why occupied columns and diagonals are tracked for fast conflict checks.

The mini-project builds an `AuditPlacementSolver`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input n is four.

Step 1: Row zero tries column zero; it is safe, so the queen is placed and all three sets record it.

Step 2: Rows advance; when a row has no safe column the recursion backtracks, removing the last queen's set keys.

Step 3: Two full placements emerge for n equal to four: columns one, three, zero, two and columns two, zero, three, one.

Step 4: Each solution is recorded as the column chosen per row.

```text

2026-10-27T00:35:00Z [INFO] Found 2 valid placements for n=4

2026-10-27T00:35:00Z [INFO] Placement (col per row): [2, 0, 3, 1]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  row 0..n-1, try cols:
    safe if c∉cols && (row-c)∉diag1 && (row+c)∉diag2
    place → recurse row+1 → unplace on backtrack
  n=4 → 2 solutions [1,3,0,2], [2,0,3,1]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
N-Queens is the classic constraint-satisfaction backtracking problem. I place one queen per row and, for each row, try every column, placing a queen only where it does not conflict with any already-placed queen. The key to making the conflict test fast is tracking three sets: the occupied columns, one diagonal family keyed by row minus column, and the other keyed by row plus column. Those two diagonal identities are the insight that turns each conflict check into a constant-time set lookup instead of a board scan.

When I place a queen I add its column and both diagonal keys, recurse to the next row, and on backtrack I remove exactly those keys. Reaching row n means all queens are placed without conflict, so I record the configuration. The pruning from the three sets keeps the real search far below the naive n-to-the-n bound.

In my project at National Bank of India, compliance needed to place n audit checkpoints on an n-by-n scheduling grid so that no two conflicted by column or diagonal time-slot, and it wanted every valid arrangement. The row-by-row backtracking with constant-time conflict sets produced all placements efficiently, which is exactly the N-Queens template applied to a scheduling constraint.
